podcast.body: Released in the summer of 1965, this song became an instant number one hit, largely due to Keith Richards' distinctive guitar riff. The band's decision to overrule Richards' desire for a horn section and instead record his guitar part through a Maestro Fuzzbox pedal on May 12, 1965, proved transformative. The track's success caused Maestro Fuzz Tone pedals to fly off the shelves, cementing the role of distortion in rock music. "When I can't get no satisfaction, was released in the summer of 1965, it was an instant hit."

podcast.body: The Rolling Stones' "Satisfaction" became a massive hit and solidified the distorted guitar sound's place at the forefront of rock music. The iconic riff, initially intended by Keith Richards to be a placeholder for a horn section and played with a Maestro Fuzz tone, was loved by the rest of the band despite Richards' preference for horns. Recorded at RCA Studios in Hollywood on May 12, 1965, the song was released four weeks later. "Another satisfaction was a hit for the Stones. Everybody wanted a Maestro Fuzz tone, but key thritchards almost didn't use that bit."

podcast.body: This song was the top song of the "epic summer of 1965" and topped the 60s ranking of Songs of the Summer. It served as the breakthrough hit for the Rolling Stones, marking their first number one in America after more than a year of falling short of their British Invasion competition. Keith Richards famously "conjured" its immortal guitar riff in a dream, and Mick Jagger's lyrics were considered scandalous for their overt sexuality and anti-commercialism. "Who, after more than a year of falling short of their British invasion competition, finally hit number one in America with a song whose immortal riff Keith Richards conjured in a dream. And whose Mick Jagger lyrics were considered scandalous for their overt sexuality and anti-commercialism."
